results.summary: This design implements and compares three different clock domain crossing synchronizers: a two flip-flop synchronizer, a recirculation mux synchronizer, and a toggle synchronizer. The user can select which synchronizer output to observe using a 3-bit selector input, and the design includes an enable control block to run each synchronizer once. External hardware is not required beyond clock and data sources to drive the inputs. The project is notable for being an educational testbed to study metastability mitigation techniques in multi-clock designs.

This design implements a 4-tap FIR filter with user-configurable coefficients, or default coefficients set to 1. It takes an input signal x[n] and produces output y[n] by multiplying the last four input samples with the coefficients and summing the results. The coefficients can be assigned via switches when the enable signal is high, and a reset sets past values to zero and coefficients to ones. External hardware includes a microcontroller to send the x[n] values, and the design is notable for being a simple digital filter implementation.

This design is an FM transmitter that takes an audio signal via I2S and modulates it onto a higher carrier frequency using a numerically controlled oscillator with a piecewise linear approximation of a sine wave. It outputs a 4-bit digital signal to an external R-2R ladder DAC to generate the analog FM signal, and also includes an optional SPI interface. The design is not intended for real on-air use and requires external filtering to comply with regulations. It is notable for its resource-efficient approximation of sine generation and its ability to produce FM signals in the broadcast band despite a lower sampling frequency.

ROTFPGA v2 is a reconfigurable logic circuit consisting of an 8x8 grid of identical tiles, each containing a NAND gate, a D flip-flop, and a buffer, with each tile individually rotatable and mirrorable via configuration. Configuration and state are managed through a scan chain, and a loop breaker mechanism helps debug combinational loops. The design supports loading and dumping state, single-stepping, and free running, and it has been tested on silicon with a provided test suite. It is notable for being a port of a larger FPGA design to TinyTapeout with significant area optimization.

This project implements an I2C slave with address 0x04, as indicated by the title and pin names. It provides 6-bit data paths to and from a master, along with control signals, but the documentation is essentially empty, so its exact functionality and usage cannot be determined. External hardware would likely include an I2C master to communicate with the device. The project is notable only for its sparse documentation and minimal description.

This is a traffic light controller implemented as a finite state machine that, when started, cycles through red, green, and yellow lights with durations of 30, 20, and 3 seconds respectively, using a clock frequency divider for timing. The design requires three external LEDs to display the lights, though they are optional. It was created for the LatinPractice Bootcamp at the University of Illinois Springfield (UIS). The project is notable for its educational context and simple, practical application.

This design is an implementation of the SAP-1 (Simple As Possible) CPU from the book 'Digital Computer Electronics' by Malvino and Brown. It executes a fixed program hard-coded in a 16x8 ROM, implementing instructions like LDA, ADD, SUB, and OUT, with the results appearing on an 8-bit output. It requires an external clock and reset signal, and the output can be observed via LEDs. The project is notable for being an educational CPU implementation that adapts the book's shared-bus architecture to CMOS-friendly design.

This design is a controller for a Pulsed Plasma Thruster (PPT) that generates a configurable number of pulses with adjustable frequency and pulse width, controllable via an I2C slave interface. It can also run with default settings using an override input, producing a pulse train at 0.25 Hz with 16 pulses. The design outputs pulse train status and a divided clock, and displays pulses on a 7-segment display. It is notable for being verified in simulation and prototyped on an FPGA, targeting space propulsion applications.

This design is a simple 8-bit adder built using RustHDL, which adds two 8-bit inputs (ui_in and uio_in) and outputs the sum on uo_out. It requires only a clock and reset signal to function, and no external hardware is needed beyond the connections. The design is notable for being implemented in RustHDL, showcasing an alternative hardware description language. It is a straightforward arithmetic building block with minimal complexity.

This design implements a Karplus-Strong string synthesis algorithm to generate plucked string sounds, with a register map configurable via SPI and audio output via I2S. It also includes two PRBS noise generators for adding noise to the string model, and displays status on a 7-segment display. The design requires an external I2S DAC or codec to output the synthesized audio. It is notable for being a digital music synthesizer implementation based on published papers and for its use of a 2x2 tile area.
